newsitem.title: USA: COR drug helps fight ischemia -study.
newsitem.headline: COR drug helps fight ischemia -study.

text.p: A new drug made by COR Therapeutics Inc has been shown to reduce the risk of heart attacks caused by blood clots, Johns Hopkins University said.
The drug, integrelin, signficantly lowered instances of reduced blood flow to the heart, or "ischemia," in patients with unstable angina, the university said in a release.
Findings of integrelin studies led by Johns Hopkins researchers were to be published in the November 1 issue of the journal Circulation and the November issue of Clinical Cardiology.
One study showed that patients receiving high integrelin doses had significantly fewer and shorter episodes of ischemia than those who received aspirin, which also can protect against heart attack.

The results also suggested women benefited more from integrelin than men. Women receiving integrelin had fewer and shorter angina attacks than women receiving aspirin. Among men, there was no significant difference in attacks between patients receiving integrelin and aspirin, Johns Hopkins said.
The other study showed integrelin provided women with significantly more protection than apirin against ischemia caused by blood platelet clots, the university said.
Platelets are cells that help blood to clot. Integrelin works by making platelets less likely to bind together and block arteries feeding the heart, it said.
There also was no increase in clotting after patients were taken off integrelin, it said.

"Our findings indicate that integrelin is well tolerated and is a potent inhibitor of platelet aggregation when compared with aspirin," Dr Steven Schulman, lead author of one of the studies and a medical professor at Johns Hopkins, said in the university release.
The study was funded in part by COR Therapeutics and the National Institutes of Health.
